extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law, legislative procedure, and political history
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material describing when constitutional conventions are appropriate, how constitutional drafting differs from legislative processes, the provenance of provisions in the Federal Constitution, and explicit Rules of the U.S. Senate plus comparative treatment of private bills and lobbying in England and America.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use a constitutional convention vs limited amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complete new constitution is to be prepared, the balance of convenience is decidedly in favour of giving the work to a convention; where it is not desired to revise the whole frame of government, the simpler and better plan is to proceed by submitting to the people specific amendments limited to particular provisions of the existing constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions are preferable for full constitutional revision because they are composed of men specially chosen for the purpose, free from ordinary administrative responsibilities and party pressures; specific amendments are preferable for limited reforms and have lately been the common method of improving State constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and composition of constitutional conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An American Constitutional Convention, being chosen for the sole purpose of drafting a constitution and having nothing to do with ordinary administration, is not necessarily elected on party hues or in obedience to party considerations. Hence men comparatively indifferent to party are sometimes elected; those seeking office for party advancement do not generally care to serve in a convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because conventions have no patronage, revenue, or administrative power, they attract public-spirited citizens and professionals averse to routine politics, producing higher levels of honesty and often superior ability compared with legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative advantages of conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the convention meets it is not, like a legislature, a body strictly organized by party. A sense of individual independence and freedom may prevail, proposals have a chance of being considered on their merits, debate has less tendency to stray off to irrelevant matters, and business advances because there are no interruptions as a legislature charged with ordinary business must expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions' single-purpose, short duration, and lack of ordinary party issues reduce popularity-hunting and permit concentrated consideration of constitutional questions; drafts are prepared with more care because they will be submitted to the people en bloc.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's ratification increases draft-care
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the constitution when drafted has to be submitted to the people gives to the convention a somewhat larger freedom for proposing what they think best than a legislature courting or fearing its constituents commonly allows itself... And as the people must accept or reject the draft en bloc ... more care is taken in preparing the draft, in clearing it of errors and repugnances, than a legislature ... bestows on the details of its measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission en bloc to popular vote incentivizes conventions to prepare a cleaner, more coherent draft; this reduces motive for populist drafting and increases attention to detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of initiative to propose constitutional amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescribed number of the citizens have been in six Western States empowered by their Constitutions to propose by means of the Initiative amendments to the Constitution, which are thereupon submitted to popular vote without the intervention either of the legislature or of a convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initiative is an alternative route to constitutional amendment distinct from legislative or convention channels, used in some states to allow citizen-proposed amendments to go directly to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum requirement in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: A QUORUM shall consist of a majority of the senators, duly chosen and sworn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic threshold rule for conducting Senate business; majority present and sworn constitutes quorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate recording of different classes of Senate proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, the executive, the confidential legislative proceedings, and the proceedings when sitting as a Court of Impeachment, shall each be recorded in a separate book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records must be kept distinct by class of proceeding to preserve confidentiality and institutional clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for yeas and nays
rubrics_metrics.description: When the yeas and nays are ordered, the names of senators shall be called alphabetically; and each senator shall, without debate, declare his assent or dissent to the question, unless excused by the Senate; and no senator shall be permitted to vote after the decision shall have been announced by the presiding officer, but may for sufficient reasons, with unanimous consent, change or withdraw his vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roll-call voting procedure with prohibition on voting after announcement except by unanimous consent to change; ensures orderly recorded votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusal from voting when declining to vote
rubrics_metrics.description: When a senator declines to vote on call of his name, he shall be required to assign his reasons therefor, and on his having assigned them, the presiding officer shall submit the question to the Senate, 'Shall the senator for the reasons assigned by him, be excused from voting?' which shall be decided without debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal process to excuse a senator from voting; preserves accountability while allowing excusal by Senate decision without debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of standing committees by ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: In the appointment of the standing committees, the Senate, unless otherwise ordered, shall proceed by ballot to appoint severally the chairman of each committee, and then, by one ballot, the other members necessary to complete the same. A majority of the whole number of votes given shall be necessary to the choice of a chairman of a standing committee, but a plurality of votes shall elect the other members thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairmen require majority support; other members elected by plurality. Promotes democratic selection within Senate for committee composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of other committees by ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: All other committees shall be appointed by ballot, unless otherwise ordered, and a plurality of votes shall appoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-standing committees selected by plurality ballot unless the Senate orders otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resumption of unfinished legislative business at subsequent sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: At the second or any subsequent session of a Congress, the legislative business which remained undetermined at the close of the next preceding session of that Congress shall be resumed and proceeded with in the same manner as if no adjournment of the Senate had taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures continuity of legislative consideration across sessions of the same Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing doors for secret discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion made and seconded to close the doors of the Senate, on the discussion of any business which may, in the opinion of a senator, require secrecy, the presiding officer shall direct the galleries to be cleared; and during the discussion of such motion the doors shall remain closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure to move into closed session when secrecy is requested; requires motion and second and presiding officer action to clear galleries.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's seat and attendance when attending the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: When the President of the United States shall meet the Senate in the Senate chamber for the consideration of executive business, he shall have a seat on the right of the presiding officer. When the Senate shall be convened by the President of the United States to any other place, the presiding officer of the Senate and the senators shall attend at the place appointed, with the necessary officers of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies ceremonial seating and attendance obligations when the President meets the Senate for executive business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearing the chamber for confidential/executive business and oath of secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting upon confidential or executive business, unless the same shall be considered in open executive session, the Senate chamber shall be cleared of all persons except the secretary, the chief clerk, the principal legislative clerk, the executive clerk, the minute and journal clerk, the sergeant-at-arms, the assistant doorkeeper, and such other officers as the presiding officer shall think necessary, and all such officers shall be sworn to secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight limits on who may remain during confidential business; specified officers must be sworn to secrecy to protect sensitive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of confidential communications and treaty proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: All confidential communications made by the President of the United States to the Senate shall be by the senators and the officers of the Senate kept secret; and all treaties which may be laid before the Senate, and all remarks, votes, and proceedings thereon, shall also be kept secret until the Senate shall, by their resolution, take off the injunction of secrecy, or unless the same shall be considered in open executive session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats certain executive communications and treaty deliberations as secret until the Senate chooses to disclose them; protects executive-Senate confidential exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for disclosure of secret Senate business
rubrics_metrics.description: Any senator or officer of the Senate who shall disclose the secret or confidential business or proceedings of the Senate shall be liable, if a senator, to suffer expulsion from the body; and if an officer, to dismissal from the service of the Senate, and to punishment for contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies severe institutional penalties (expulsion, dismissal, contempt) for unauthorized disclosure to enforce secrecy rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty ratification voting thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: On the final question to advise and consent to the ratification of a treaty in the form agreed to, the concurrence of two-thirds of the senators present shall be necessary to determine it in the affirmative; but all other motions and questions upon a treaty shall be decided by a majority vote, except a motion to postpone indefinitely, which shall be decided by a vote of two-thirds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes final treaty ratification (two-thirds) from ordinary treaty-related motions (majority), with an elevated threshold for indefinite postponement (two-thirds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral and timing rules for nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: When nominations shall be made by the President of the United States to the Senate, they shall, unless otherwise ordered, be referred to appropriate committees; and the final question on every nomination shall be, 'Will the Senate advise and consent to this nomination?' Which question shall not be put on the same day on which the nomination is received, nor on the day on which it may be reported by a committee, unless by unanimous consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures nominations are considered by committee and prevents immediate floor votes on the day of receipt or committee report absent unanimous consent, allowing time for consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy rules for nomination deliberations and handling of charges
rubrics_metrics.description: All information communicated or remarks made by a senator, when acting upon nominations, concerning the character or qualifications of the person nominated, also all votes upon any nomination, shall be kept secret. If, however, charges shall be made against a person nominated, the committee may, in its discretion, notify such nominee thereof, but the name of the person making such charges shall not be disclosed. The fact that a nomination has been made, or that it has been confirmed or rejected, shall not be regarded as a secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects confidential evaluation and voting on nominations while allowing committees discretion to notify nominees of charges without revealing accusers' identities; the existence or outcome of a nomination is public.

rubrics_metrics.name: English private bill notice and preliminary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In England a broad distinction is drawn between public bills and local or private bills. ... Notice is required to be given of such a bill by advertisement nearly three months before the usual date of the meeting of Parliament and copies must be deposited some weeks before the opening of the session. The second reading is usually granted as a matter of course; and after second reading, instead of being, like a public bill, considered in committee of the whole House, it goes (if opposed) to a private bill committee consisting (usually) of four members, who take evidence regarding it from the promoters and opponents, and hear counsel argue for and against its preamble and its clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private bills in England follow distinct, quasi-judicial procedures including long pre-notice/filing periods and committee hearings with counsel and evidence, reflecting their local/personal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary claims against the Crown in England
rubrics_metrics.description: Pecuniary claims against the Government are in England not raised by way of private bill. They are presented in the courts by a proceeding called a petition of right, the Crown allowing itself to be sued by one of its subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct legal remedy (petition of right) exists in England for monetary claims against the government instead of legislative private bills.

rubrics_metrics.name: American handling of private bills
rubrics_metrics.description: In America no such difference of treatment as the above exists between public and private bills; all are dealt with in substantially the same way by the usual legislative methods. A bill of a purely local or personal nature gets its second reading as a matter of course, is similarly referred to the appropriate committee (which may hear evidence regarding it, but does not hear counsel), is considered and if necessary amended by the committee, is, if time permits, reported back to the House, and there takes its chance among the jostling crowd of other bills; Fridays, however, being specially set apart for the consideration of private business. There is a calendar of private bills, and those which get a place early upon it have a chance of passing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American practice treats private bills like public bills procedurally (committee referral, amendment, reporting) with scheduling and calendar position strongly affecting prospects for passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of private bills in Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Private bills in Congress include pension bills, bills for satisfying some claim of an individual against the Federal Government (though reduced by the Court of Claims), and bills for dispensing in particular cases with a variety of administrative statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional private bills cover a broader range of personal relief measures than English practice, reflecting different institutional choices about legislative versus judicial/administrative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical realities of committee-dominated legislative process in America
rubrics_metrics.description: All business goes before committees, not only private bills but public bills, often involving great pecuniary interests. To give a bill a fair chance of passing, the committee must be induced to report in favour of it. The committees have no quasi-judicial rules of procedure, but inquire into and amend bills in their uncontrolled discretion, upon such evidence or other statements as they choose to admit or use. Bills are advocated before committees by persons not belonging to any recognized and legally regulated body. The committees, both in the State legislatures and in the Federal House of Representatives, are largely composed of new men, unused to the exercise of the powers entrusted to them, though in the House of Representatives the chairman is a person of some experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes practical criteria for legislative success in the American system: committee influence is decisive; lack of formalized quasi-judicial procedures and variable committee experience mean advocates must know how to influence committees effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and legitimacy of lobbying activities
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Lobby' is the name given in America to persons, not being members of a legislature, who undertake to influence its members, and thereby to secure the passing of bills. The name does not necessarily impute any improper motive or conduct. Lobbying by no means implies in all cases the use of money to affect legislation. A measure which it is desired to pass ... may be urged upon members of the legislative body in every form of influence except the pecuniary one. By casual interviews, by informal conversation, by formal presentation of facts and arguments, by printed appeals in pamphlet form, by newspaper communications and leading articles, by personal introductions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that lobbying is a range of advocacy practices—many non-corrupt—that arise from the need to present facts and arguments to legislatures; distinguishes legitimate advocacy from pecuniary corruption.
